amendments.rule: **A purpose `לְ` + infinitive construct recast as a finite clause gives the complementizer to the preposition and the supplied subject and modal to the infinitive.** The ASV writes *that men may bring*, *that I may be glorified*. This is rule 48's division outside the privative `מִן`, and for the same reason: the complementizer is what the preposition contributes, while a supplied subject pronoun and a separately written modal belong to the verb, as rule 17 keeps a subject pronoun with its verb. The corpus puts the *that* on the preposition in 28 units across 17 chapters and never on the infinitive, so this too is settled. Where the ASV writes no English word at all for the preposition there is nothing to place, and the `לְ` goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **Read that as no word, not as no complementizer.** The complementizer is what a finite recasting spends on the preposition, but a recasting that makes the infinitive an English gerund or a bare verbal noun writes an ordinary preposition in that same position, and that word is the `לְ`'s on the same terms: `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ` → *by keeping his covenant*, `לִשְׁלֹחַ מַלְאָכָיו` → *in sending his ambassadors*, `לְהָפֵר בְּרִית` → *by breaking the covenant*, `לָצֶקֶת` → *for casting*, `לֶאֱכֹל` → *an end of eating*. The corpus aligns a `לְ` before an infinitive construct to a written *to* in 583 units, to *that* in 81, and to *for*, *in*, *of*, *by*, *after* or *when* in 53 more, against 527 marked `unrepresented`; the two groups do not disagree, because every unrepresented one is a recasting that writes no function word at all — *left off building*, *the building of the house*. So ask whether a word is written before reaching for rule 40, and do not read the gerund itself as the recasting that silences the preposition. **Where two such `לְ` + infinitive phrases stand in one clause and the ASV writes one complementizer and one preposition, count them as this rule's last sentence directs rather than taking them in linear order.** `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ לְעָמְדָהּ` → *that by keeping his covenant it might stand* gives *by* to the `לְ` of the gerund and *that* to the `לְ` whose infinitive the finite clause renders: the ASV fronts the complementizer ahead of the gerund adjunct, and that reordering says nothing about which preposition it answers to. **A temporal preposition before an infinitive construct is read the same way.** Where `בְּ` or `כְּ` + infinitive is recast as a finite temporal clause — `בְּחֻמָּם` → *When they are heated*, `בְּלֶכְתּוֹ` → *when he went*, `כְּבֹאֲךָ` → *When thou comest*, `כְּכַלֹּתְךָ` → *when thou hast made an end* — the preposition takes the *when*, the infinitive keeps the verb, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18. The corpus aligns `בְּ` to *when* in 45 units, so the temporal case is settled on the same footing as the purpose case. Read the preposition that is present rather than its lemma: a `לְ` heading such a phrase goes the same way even where its object is the noun rather than the infinitive, as in `לְקוֹל תִּתּוֹ` → *When he uttereth his voice*. **But only a preposition that still has an English word to take can take it.** Where no preposition is present and the construct relation itself is what the English *when* realizes, rule 19 puts that word on the *nomen rectum*, which is the infinitive: `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ` → *at the time when it is trodden* gives *at the time* to `עֵת` and *when ... is trodden* to the infinitive. **And a preposition on which the ASV has already spent its own English word is in the same position as an absent one.** Where the preposition heads a construct noun, the ASV writes a word for that preposition and a second temporal word besides, the second answers to the construct relation and not to the preposition, so rule 19 puts it on the *nomen rectum*: `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` → *in the day when they shall make it* gives *in* to the `בְּ` and *the day* to `יוֹם`, leaving *when they shall make* to the infinitive, whose own suffix takes the pronoun rule 18 gives it. Count the ASV's function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s and rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s: a preposition holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, and giving it both would leave the construct's relation unrendered against rule 2. **Where no preposition stands before the infinitive construct at all, the English infinitive marker *to* belongs to the infinitive's own unit and is never `added`.** English writes no bare infinitive complement, so that word is what the infinitive itself licenses, exactly as rule 15 gives a supplied *a* to the noun that licenses it and rule 46 gives a supplied *them that* to a bare participle: `מֵאֵן בִּלְעָם הֲלֹךְ עִמָּנוּ` → *Balaam refuseth* ***to come*** *with us* and `הֲיָכוֹל אוּכַל דַּבֵּר מְאוּמָה` → *have I now any power at all* ***to speak*** *anything* each give the *to* to the infinitive, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24. Read whether a preposition is present before reaching for this sentence, since one and the same infinitive is read both ways in one chapter: `לַהֲלֹךְ עִמָּכֶם` → *to go with you* gives the written *to* to the `לְ` and only *go* to `הֲלֹךְ`, while the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds both words. And this reaches only a *to* the ASV has written: a modal's bare complement — *cannot go beyond* — has none to place, and a preposition the recasting leaves unrendered is `unrepresented` under rule 40 as before.
amendments.why: Rule 52 governs `לְ` (and `בְּ`/`כְּ`) before an infinitive construct in every direction except the one where no preposition stands at all, and NUM.22 met that case twice with the same infinitive the rule's own machinery handles elsewhere: 22.13 `לַהֲלֹךְ` → *to go* (le takes the written to) against 22.14 `הֲלֹךְ` → *to come* and 22.38 `דַּבֵּר` → *to speak*, where nothing is present to answer for the marker. Left unstated, the next pass reads rule 30's 'reserve added for English that no morpheme licenses' and marks the marker `added`, or hunts for an absent preposition. The amendment states the answer in rule 52's own terms and cites the two rules whose reasoning it borrows, and the corpus contradicts nothing: its 583 `לְ` → *to* units are all written prepositions, a different case.

amendments.rule: Where the ASV's recasting leaves a preposition with no English word — the impersonal `קרא לְ` + suffix rendered as a personal passive, `וְקֹרָא לָךְ` → *and thou shalt be called*, or a dative `לְ` + suffix rendered as a bare English indirect object, `תְּנָה לִּי` → *give me* — the preposition is its own `unrepresented` unit and its suffix takes the English pronoun that realizes it, including a subject pronoun. This is rule 21's recasting clause outside the resultative `הָיָה לְ`, and it is the case where rule 18's *possessive or object* is not the whole range. **The `לְ` is the commonest case, not the condition.** The same recasting silences any preposition it leaves nothing to say: `צוּר עַל` → *besieged Tirzah* and `צִוִּיתִי עָלֶיךָ` → *commanded thee* leave `עַל` bare, `אֶל` goes the same way before a bare English object, and a `בְּ` whose object the ASV promotes to a direct object — *blew the trumpet* — keeps nothing either. Read the condition, not the lemma: ask whether the ASV spends an English word on what that preposition contributes. **And a word the ASV writes as part of a neighbouring morpheme's own compound rendering is not a word spent on the preposition.** Where a Hebrew adverb or noun standing beside the preposition is rendered by an English expression written in two or three words, that expression belongs whole to the morpheme it renders, exactly as rule 30 reads its one-English-word condition as one rendering rather than one token, and the preposition takes a word only where the ASV has written one for its own relation. `הֶחָצֵר סָבִיב לַמִּשְׁכָּן` → *the court round about the tabernacle* gives *round about* whole to `סָבִיב`, headed on *round* under rule 24, and leaves the `לְ` `unrepresented`, exactly as the coordinated `וְלַמִּזְבֵּחַ` beside it is left. Do not divide such an expression to give a present preposition something to hold: rule 11 gives each morpheme the English it licenses, and half of another morpheme's fixed rendering is not English this one licenses. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the word and ask whether the preposition's own relation has gone unstated, or whether only the neighbouring expression has been broken in two. The corpus renders `סָבִיב` by *round about* headed on *round* in 144 units and by a bare *round* in two, one of them hedged and the other a doubled adverb for which the ASV writes a separate word for each occurrence, and it reads the whole compound as the adverb's own in four of the five units where a determined preposition follows it. **But read whether the preposition's own object is rendered at all before silencing it.** Every case above is one where the ASV writes English for what the preposition governs and leaves only the relation unstated — *besieged Tirzah*, *commanded thee*, *blew the trumpet*, *give me*, *round about the tabernacle*. Where instead the governed noun is itself left with no English of its own, and a single English word carries the predicate, the preposition and that noun together, rule 30's one-rendering condition is met and this rule does not reach it: the contiguous morphemes share one unit headed on the one carrying the lexeme, rather than one rendered morpheme standing beside others marked `unrepresented`, which is what rule 30 forbids for a fixed expression and what rule 22 forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused word. `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* gives *it displease* to `רַע`, `בְּ` and `עַיִן` in one unit headed on the verb, while the suffix keeps the *thee* written for it under rule 18, exactly as `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses under rule 30. Contiguity is that rule's condition and it is the limit here too: `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded*, where the subject or the object stands between, is split by rule 2 and its preposition is `unrepresented` as before. Test by subtraction — drop the English word and ask whether the preposition's noun as well as its relation has gone unsaid; where the noun keeps a word of its own, this rule governs and the preposition is `unrepresented`.
amendments.why: Rule 40's *silences any preposition it leaves nothing to say* was read at NUM.22.34 as silencing `בְּ` in `רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *displease thee* and, with rule 22, dropping `עַיִן` beside it — three morphemes, one rendered, two unrepresented, which is the shape rule 30 explicitly rejects for a fixed expression rendered by one English word. The boundary was already latent in rule 40's own examples: in every one of them (*besieged Tirzah*, *commanded thee*, *blew the trumpet*, *give me*, *round about the tabernacle*) the ASV writes English for what the preposition governs, so only the relation is unstated. NUM.22 supplies both sides of the contrast in a single verse — the ethical dative of `אָשׁוּבָה לִּי` keeps rule 40 because its suffix takes *me*, while `בְּעֵינֶיךָ` does not because its noun takes nothing — and the chapter fuses every other one-word expression (`מִפְּנֵי`, `לִקְרָאת`, `לְנֶגֶד`, `מֵעֵבֶר`, `כַּאֲשֶׁר`, `לֹא אוּכַל`). Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the over-broad sentence is qualified where a later pass will read it, and bounded by rule 30's contiguity condition so it cannot be turned on `גָּדַל ... מִן`.

conventions: yasap hiphil with a complementary infinitive (22.15, 22.19, 22.25, 22.26): the finite yasap takes only the repetition word the ASV writes for it - yet, again, further, more - and the infinitive keeps the lexical verb, each morpheme taking the word written for it under rule 2. A clause auxiliary goes with the finite form (22.19, will ... more); a subject pronoun supplied for the recast English clause goes with the infinitive that carries the English verb (22.25, he smote ... again), as rules 18 and 48 keep a supplied infinitival subject with its infinitive.

A fused preposition plus a nominal preposition is headed on the second morpheme in this chapter - mimmul -> over against (22.5), le-neged -> before (22.32) - read as the element carrying content under rule 23's first sentence rather than as the pure function pair its me-'al example governs. This matches the chapter's heading of mippene, li-pne, liqra't and me-'eber on their construct nouns. Both units name the competing head in their notes, and no target edge depends on the choice.

A compound proper name arriving as two source tokens is aligned token by token rather than fused: qiryat huzot -> Kiriath | huzoth (22.39), with the supplied unto of the directional accusative going to the first token under rule 33. Where the ASV translates such a name instead of transliterating it, the pair is read as construct plus rectum: bamot ba'al -> the high places of Baal (22.41), bamot taking into the high places (rules 31, 33) and ba'al the of Baal (rule 19). The ASV's margin, Or, Bamoth-baal, corroborates the translated reading without deciding it, by rule 7.

zeh in the counting formula zeh shalosh regalim takes the plural these the ASV writes for it (22.28, 22.32, 22.33). The singular demonstrative is not left unrepresented and the plural determiner is not added, since no other morpheme in the phrase answers to it; the numeral and regalim keep three and times.

Do not divide such an expression to give a present preposition something to hold: rule 11 gives each morpheme the English it licenses, and half of another morpheme's fixed rendering is not English this one licenses. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the word and ask whether the preposition's own relation has gone unstated, or whether only the neighbouring expression has been broken in two. Where instead the governed noun is itself left with no English of its own, and a single English word carries the predicate, the preposition and that noun together, rule 30's one-rendering condition is met and this rule does not reach it: the contiguous morphemes share one unit headed on the one carrying the lexeme, rather than one rendered morpheme standing beside others marked `unrepresented`, which is what rule 30 forbids for a fixed expression and what rule 22 forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused word. `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* gives *it displease* to `רַע`, `בְּ` and `עַיִן` in one unit headed on the verb, while the suffix keeps the *thee* written for it under rule 18, exactly as `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses under rule 30. Contiguity is that rule's condition and it is the limit here too: `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded*, where the subject or the object stands between, is split by rule 2 and its preposition is `unrepresented` as before. Test by subtraction — drop the English word and ask whether the preposition's noun as well as its relation has gone unsaid; where the noun keeps a word of its own, this rule governs and the preposition is `unrepresented`.
amended.why: Rule 40's *silences any preposition it leaves nothing to say* was read at NUM.22.34 as silencing `בְּ` in `רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *displease thee* and, with rule 22, dropping `עַיִן` beside it — three morphemes, one rendered, two unrepresented, which is the shape rule 30 explicitly rejects for a fixed expression rendered by one English word. The boundary was already latent in rule 40's own examples: in every one of them (*besieged Tirzah*, *commanded thee*, *blew the trumpet*, *give me*, *round about the tabernacle*) the ASV writes English for what the preposition governs, so only the relation is unstated. NUM.22 supplies both sides of the contrast in a single verse — the ethical dative of `אָשׁוּבָה לִּי` keeps rule 40 because its suffix takes *me*, while `בְּעֵינֶיךָ` does not because its noun takes nothing — and the chapter fuses every other one-word expression (`מִפְּנֵי`, `לִקְרָאת`, `לְנֶגֶד`, `מֵעֵבֶר`, `כַּאֲשֶׁר`, `לֹא אוּכַל`). Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the over-broad sentence is qualified where a later pass will read it, and bounded by rule 30's contiguity condition so it cannot be turned on `גָּדַל ... מִן`.

report: Checked every multi-treatment bucket in the candidate table. Almost all are the ASV rendering one word differently in different contexts (waw to And/and/but/Then/So/therefore/Now/with/either-or; ki to for/because/that/surely; min to from/of/out of/than/all), or a difference the source licenses. Worked cases: halok takes a bare 'go' after a written le (22.13), 'to come' with no preposition at all (22.14), 'coming' after min (22.16); liqra't fuses to 'against' where the ASV writes one word (22.34) and splits into 'to' + 'meet' where it writes two (22.36), which is rule 30's own condition; the article takes a demonstrative or possessive determiner only where no demonstrative pronoun or suffix stands in the phrase (22.4, 22.8, 22.19, 22.27, 22.32 against 22.6, 22.9, 22.17, 22.30). None of these is a split.

One genuine error, which the candidate table is structurally blind to because both offending morphemes are unrepresented and so appear in no lemma group: NUM.22.34 'im-ra' be-'eyneyka -> 'if it displease thee' gave 'it displease' to ra' alone, marking be unrepresented under rule 40 and 'ayin unrepresented under rule 22. One English word carries all three contiguous morphemes, which is rule 30's fusion and exactly the shape that rule forbids ('rather than one rendered morpheme beside others marked unrepresented'). Patched: s023+s024+s025 share one unit headed on ra' / displease, and the suffix keeps the 'thee' written for it. Nothing outside that unit moves.

BSB disagreements. The R x14, Td x9 and Sh x6 blocks and the object-marker rows are the documented convention difference: BSB attaches prepositions, articles, the paragogic he and 'et to their host words, while this chapter follows rules 16, 27, 29, 32 and 40. The two waws are right as aligned (the ASV writes no connective at 22.11, and 22.36's is the apodosis waw that rule 14 leaves unrepresented where the ASV opens the clause bare). 22.30 'alay is right: the ASV writes one 'which' for the antecedent, so the resumptive suffix takes nothing (rules 22, 43). Only 22.34 'eyney was a genuine error, and it is now fixed.

Examined and left. (a) The source head of mimmul (22.5) and le-neged (22.32) sits on the second morpheme; that is consistent across the chapter and matches how it heads mippene, liqra't and me-'eber on their construct nouns, but it sits against rule 23's me-'al example. Both notes name the competing head and no edge moves, so it is recorded as a convention rather than patched. (b) 22.25 puts the subject pronoun 'he' on the infinitive while 22.19 puts the auxiliary 'will' on the finite yasap: rules 18 and 48 license a supplied infinitival subject on its infinitive, so the pair is not a split, and the adverbial word is on the finite yasap in all four occurrences (22.15, 22.19, 22.25, 22.26).

The three added units stand. The two supplied subordinators at 22.6 open clauses the Hebrew leaves asyndetic (rule 55), and the supplied 'saying' at 22.10 has no le'mor behind it. They do not conflict with 22.4's 'all that is round about us', where the relative frame supplies the noun-phrase frame a bare adverbial nominal needs (rules 41, 46) rather than subordinating a written finite clause.

Four conventions recorded and two amendments returned. The amendments are the two places the contract met a case it had not considered: rule 52 says nothing about the English infinitive marker where no preposition stands at all (22.14, 22.38), and rule 40's 'silences any preposition it leaves nothing to say' is over-broad for the 22.34 idiom. Every example rule 40 already carries is one whose governed noun the ASV does render, so the boundary is drawn there rather than by a new rule pointing back at it.
